talk.title: My timeline
talk.task: Give Claude 4 dates from your life. Make simple past and present perfect sentences about them.
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English writing partner. Ask me for 4 important years in my life and what happened (for example: 2019: I started university). Then ask me to write one simple past sentence and one present perfect sentence (with since or for) about each. Check that I use simple past with a finished time and present perfect for things that are still true.

items.title: Started before, still going
lines: have / has been + verb-ing.
It tells how long an activity has been going on.

examples.text: I have been sitting here for two hours.

items.title: Right now vs. how long

examples.text: I am sitting at my desk.
I have been sitting at my desk since seven o'clock.
It's been raining all day.

items.tip: since / for / all day → have been + -ing. Never: I am sitting here for two hours.

items.text: She ___ for the bus for 15 minutes.
items.why: for 15 minutes = how long → has been waiting.

items.title: No -ing for state verbs
lines: know, have (own), like, be: no -ing.
Use the present perfect.

examples.text: I've known Alex since he was a child.

items.text: Joe ___ the same bike for 20 years.
items.why: have = own is a state verb → has had.

items.title: Sometimes both are OK
lines: live, work, teach, study, wear, play: habits.
Both forms mean the same.

examples.text: How long have you lived here?
How long have you been living here?

items.title: No time word = lately
lines: No since or for? It means recently.

examples.text: I've been thinking about looking for a different job.

lines: have / has been + -ing: how long an activity has been going on.
State verbs (know, have, like, be): have + past participle.

examples.text: It's been raining all day.
I've known Alex since he was a child.

items.text: Anita is at the bus stop.

She has been waiting for the bus for 15 minutes.

items.text: It's been raining all day. It's = ?
It's still raining right now. It's = ?

options: what have you been up to

items.say: Not too much. I've been taking it easy.
Glad to hear you haven't been working too hard.
By the way, how are your parents? I haven't seen them for a while.
items.why: for a while, up to now → haven't seen.

options: How long have they been retired
items.why: How long … up to now → have they been.

talk.title: What have you been doing?
talk.task: Claude asks why you look tired, wet, happy… Answer with “I've been …-ing”.
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. I am practicing the present perfect progressive. Ask me short questions one at a time, such as: Why are you shivering? Why are you so tired? What took you so long? Why are your hands dirty? Why are you smiling? I must invent an answer with 'I've been + verb-ing' (for example: I've been standing outside in the cold). Check that I use have been + -ing.

talk.title: Write a product review
talk.task: Write a short review of something you own. Use “I have had…” and “I have been …-ing”.
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English writing partner. Ask me to write a short product review (3-4 sentences) of something I own, like a phone, shoes or headphones. I must use the present perfect at least once (I have had it for ...) and the present perfect progressive at least once (I have been using it ...). Check those two tenses and tell me one thing I did well.

items.title: Two past events. Which was first?
lines: had + past participle = the earlier one.

examples.text: Sam came at 10:00. Ann had already left.

items.text: By the time Sam came, Ann had already left.

items.title: by the time
lines: by the time + simple past → the other verb takes had.

examples.text: By the time Sam came, Ann had already left.

items.title: before / after: both are OK

examples.text: Sam had left before Ann came.
After the guests had left, I went to bed.
Sam left before Ann came.
After the guests left, I went to bed.

items.tip: before and after already show the order. So simple past is fine too.

items.text: I was late. When I got to class, the quiz ___.
items.why: It started before I got there → had started.

items.title: Telling what someone said
lines: She said it in the past? Go one step back.

examples.text: “I lost my keys.”
Jenny said that she had lost her keys.

items.title: Short form: 'd
lines: had → 'd after I, you, he, she, it, we, they.
items.tip: I'd left = I had left. I'd like to leave = I would like.

lines: had + past participle: finished before another past time.
With before / after, simple past is OK too.

examples.text: By the time Sam came, Ann had already left.
Jenny said that she had lost her keys.

items.text: The teacher stood up. Someone had knocked on the classroom door.
I looked at the board. The teacher had written my name there.
Sam came at 10:00. Ann had already left.
Sam had left before Ann came.
items.why: had left + before → Sam was first.

items.text: After the guests had left, I went to bed.
items.why: after + had left → the guests were first.

items.text: Bill felt great that evening. Earlier in the day, he had caught three fish.
items.why: had caught = earlier in the day.

items.text: I woke up with a headache, but I ___ better after I took some medicine.
items.why: The later event → simple past: felt.

items.text: I felt better after I ___ some medicine.
items.why: With after, both took and had taken are OK.

items.text: I was late for my first class. The teacher ___ a quiz when I got to class.
items.why: Before I got there → had already given.

items.text: The teacher had already given a quiz when I ___ to class.
items.why: The later event → simple past: got.

items.text: It was raining really hard when I ___ home this morning.
items.why: A finished event this morning → left.

items.text: My shoes were soaked when I ___ to work.
items.why: A finished event → simple past: got.

items.text: Fortunately, by the time I ___ ready to leave, they had dried.
items.why: by the time + simple past: was.

items.text: By the time I was ready to leave, my shoes ___.
items.why: by the time … → had already dried.

items.text: I ___ a fantastic lunch to take to work.
items.why: The story's events → simple past: made.

items.text: I ___ it in the staff fridge this morning.
items.why: this morning → simple past: put, put, put.

items.text: I never ___ a chance to eat it.
When I went to the fridge, someone ___ it.
items.why: Before I went there → had already eaten.

items.text: Jenny: “I lost my keys.” → Jenny said that she ___ her keys.
items.why: Reported in the past → one step back: had lost.

items.text: Bill felt great that evening. Earlier in the day, he ___ three fish.
They ___ a delicious picnic near the lake earlier that day.
items.why: had + part 3 of have = had had.

items.text: I'd left before you called. I'd = ?
I'd like to leave now. I'd = ?
I got ready to pay the bill, but when I ___ in my purse…
…I discovered that I ___ my wallet.
items.why: It happened before I looked → had forgotten.

items.text: I ___ so embarrassed.
items.why: The story's event → simple past: felt.

items.text: My friend generously ___ to pay my part of the bill.
During my lunch break, I ___ to go to the art museum.
I ___ any of Picasso's paintings before I went there.
items.why: Before that visit → had never seen.

items.text: I had never seen any of Picasso's paintings before I ___ there.
items.why: The later event → simple past: went.

items.text: Yesterday at the airport, I ___ into Rick Collins, an old friend of mine.
I ___ to him in years.
At first, I ___ him.
items.why: At that moment → simple past: didn't recognize.

items.text: I didn't recognize him because he ___ a great deal of weight.
items.why: It happened before the meeting → had lost.

items.text: By the time Sam came, Ann ___.
items.why: by the time … → had already left.

items.text: After the guests ___, I went to bed.
items.why: With after, both had left and left are OK.

talk.title: A terrible day
talk.task: Tell Claude about a bad day (real or invented). Use “had already…” two times.
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. I am practicing the past perfect. Ask me to tell a short story about a day when things went wrong (real or invented). Help me with questions like: What had already happened when you arrived? What had you forgotten? I should use the simple past for the main events and 'had + past participle' for things that happened earlier. Check that tense choice.

items.title: had gets tiny
lines: In fast speech, had sounds like 'd.
Tap to hear it.

items.title: 'd = had or would?
lines: Look at the next verb.

examples.text: I'd gotten sick the day before.
I'd like to try that.

items.tip: Past participle next → had. Simple verb next → would.

items.text: We'd misread the bus schedule. We'd = ?
items.why: misread is a past participle here → had.

items.title: Main verb had stays long
lines: had = owned or ate? Never short.

items.text: I'd kind of like to try that. I'd = ?
items.why: like is a simple verb → would.

lines: 'd + past participle = had. 'd + simple verb = would.
Main verb had is never short: The dog had a bone.

examples.text: Joe had already heard the story.
I'd like to try that.

items.say: I'm sorry I missed the appointment. I'd written down the wrong date.
We knew we were running late. We'd misread the bus schedule.
Sorry. I wanted to come to your party, but my family'd already made other plans.
Thanks for asking! I'd love to come next time.
items.why: love is a simple verb → would.

items.say: She'd already eaten when I called.
We'd like to see you soon.
items.why: like is a simple verb → would.

items.text: My friend Tom ___ a base jumper. He jumps off buildings for fun.
Last year he jumped off a skyscraper. Tom and his team ___ planned it for over a year.
Family and friends ___ told him he was crazy, but that didn't change his mind.
I wanted to watch, but I ___ gotten sick the day before.
Tom said it was the most thrilling experience he ___ ever had.
I ___ kind of like to try something like that, but I'm afraid of heights.
items.why: like is a simple verb → would like.

items.say: The kids'd stayed up too late. They were late for school.
The kids'd like to stay up late. There's no school tomorrow.
items.why: like is a simple verb → would.

items.say: You're a new student, aren't you? How long've you been in this country?
items.why: Up to now, with you → have.

items.say: You left your job? How long'd you been there?
You're looking for Jack? Jack's left. He isn't here.
items.why: left is part 3, result now → has.

items.say: We were looking for Sam, but he'd left by the time we got there.
items.why: by the time we got there → had.

items.say: The kids've stayed up too late. They need to go to bed.
Since we're teachers, we have the summers off. We'd like to travel to Africa next.
items.why: like is a simple verb → would.

items.say: We'd wanted to travel with my parents on our last trip, but they became ill.
items.why: wanted (part 3), before a past event → had.

items.say: Unfortunately, my phone died when we were lost. I'd forgotten to recharge it.
items.why: forgotten is part 3, before it died → had.

items.say: My phone's dead, and I've forgotten to bring the charger.

items.title: Going on before a past moment
lines: had been + verb-ing.
How long, before something else in the past.

examples.text: Eric finally came at six o'clock. I had been waiting for him since four-thirty.

items.title: Up to now vs. up to then

examples.text: I have been waiting for Jack since 5:00. And I'm still here.

right.label: had been -ing: up to a past time

examples.text: I had been waiting for Jack since 5:00. Then I left.

items.tip: Is the story in the past (came, got, was)? → had been.

items.text: The police ___ for the criminal for two years before they caught him.
items.why: Before a past event (caught) → had been looking.

items.title: You could still see it
lines: The activity had just stopped.
The result was still there.

examples.text: Her hair was still wet because she had been swimming.
His eyes were red because he had been crying.

items.title: Telling what someone said
lines: have been -ing → had been -ing.
chips: have been waiting → had been waiting

examples.text: “I have been waiting for you.”
Lia told me that she had been waiting for me.

lines: had been + -ing: how long, before another past time.
have been + -ing: how long, up to now.

examples.text: I had been waiting for him since four-thirty.
Her hair was wet because she had been swimming.

items.text: I have been waiting for Jack since 5:00.
items.why: have been = up to now. Still waiting.

items.text: I had been waiting for Jack since 5:00.
items.why: had been = up to a past moment.

options: It's hot. I think I'll go inside.
But I got too hot and came inside.

items.text: I had been working outside for almost an hour.
options: It's hot. I think I'll go inside.
But I got too hot and came inside.
items.why: had been = before a past event.

items.text: When Judy got home, her hair was still wet because she ___.
items.why: Before she got home (past) → had been swimming.

items.text: I went to Ed's house after the funeral. His eyes were red because he ___.
items.why: Before I saw him (past) → had been crying.

items.text: Lia: “I have been waiting for you.” → Lia told me that she ___ for me.

options: Ryan had been researching a topic when he decided to change majors.
Ryan had researched several topics, but then he decided to change majors.
Ryan has researched several different topics.

items.why: It was midnight = past → had been.

items.text: Jack couldn't answer the teacher because he ___ for the last ten minutes.
items.why: Before a past moment (couldn't) → had been.

items.text: Jack ___ a lot. I wonder if he's in love.
items.why: Lately, up to now → has been.

items.text: Wake up! You ___ long enough. It's time to get up.
items.why: Up to now → have been sleeping.

items.text: When I woke up, I didn't know where I was. I ___ soundly.
items.why: Before I woke up (past) → had been.

items.why: Before a past event (transferred) → had been.

talk.title: I had been …-ing when…
talk.task: Finish Claude's story starters with “had been + -ing”.
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. I am practicing the past perfect progressive. Give me one situation at a time in the past, such as: 'When I saw Sara, her eyes were red. Why?' or 'Tom was very tired when he got home. Why?' I answer with 'had been + verb-ing' (for example: She had been crying). Check that I use had been + -ing.

items.title: Two perfect machines
lines: have / has + part 3 → up to now.
had + part 3 → before a past time.

items.title: Add been + -ing for how long
lines: have been + -ing → how long, up to now.
had been + -ing → how long, up to then.

items.title: Small word, big clue

examples.text: Mr. Sanchez has taught at this school for nine years.
Ms. Lincoln taught at this school for nine years.

items.tip: has taught → he is still there. taught → she is not there now.

items.text: Carlos has been living in Chicago for five years. Does he live there now?
items.why: has been living = still true now.

lines: have / has + part 3: up to now. had + part 3: before a past time.
been + -ing: how long. Simple past: finished.

examples.text: Mr. Sanchez has taught here for nine years.
Sam had left the room when I walked in.

items.text: When the rain stopped, Gloria was riding her bike to work. When the rain stopped, Paul jumped on his bike and rode to work.
items.why: was riding = already on the bike in the rain.
items.ask: Who got wet on the way to work?

items.text: Ms. Lincoln taught at this school for nine years. Mr. Sanchez has taught at this school for nine years.
items.ask: Who is teaching at this school now?

items.text: Alice was opening the door when the doorbell rang. George walked to the door after the doorbell rang.
items.why: was opening = already at the door before the bell.
items.ask: Who had been expecting a visitor?

items.text: Donna lived in Chicago for five years. Carlos has been living in Chicago for five years.
items.why: has been living = up to now.

items.text: Jane drank some lemonade because she had been working outside. Sue drank some lemonade because she was working outside.

items.ask: Who did I see when I came into the room?

items.text: Ken went to the store because he was running out of food. Ann went to the store because she had run out of food.
items.why: was running out = he still had some food.
items.ask: Who is better at planning ahead?

items.text: Jack had been studying Spanish since elementary school when he moved to Peru. Robert has been studying Spanish since elementary school.
items.why: has been studying = up to now.

items.text: You need to stay calm now. The plane ___ just hitting some turbulence.
Oh, no! I ___ lost my passport! It's not in my bag.

items.text: While we ___ traveling in Europe last summer, we met people from around the world.
items.why: In progress in the past, we → were.

items.why: In my life up to now → have never tried.

items.text: I ___ never tried frog legs until I visited France.
I ___ getting worried when you texted.
items.why: In progress in the past, I → was.

items.text: I was afraid you ___ taken the wrong subway.
items.why: Before a past moment (was afraid) → had.

items.text: People are saying that the weather ___ never been so hot and humid.
items.why: Up to now, the weather = it → has.

items.text: The first person I saw in Tokyo was a student I ___ taught several years before.
items.why: several years before that → had taught.

items.text: William ___ planned to leave for Asia on Tuesday when his sister called with bad news.
Their parents ___ been in a car accident.
Travel ___ becoming harder for my grandfather now.
He ___ lost his ability to walk and needs to use a wheelchair.
items.why: The result is now, he → has.

items.text: I ___ just found the tour podcasts you mentioned. Do you want to subscribe?

items.say: Kristi and her husband have had several conversations in the past few months about changing careers.
options: They have thought about changing careers.
They changed careers a few months ago.

items.say: Kristi has been taking a web design class since January.
options: Kristi knows how to design websites.
Kristi is learning how to design websites.

items.say: Eric has been designing websites for small companies since last year.
options: Eric designed websites only in college.
items.why: has been designing = up to now.

options: Eric wants his parents to start working for him.

items.text: My parents ___ in the 1950s.
items.why: in the 1950s = finished time → simple past.

items.text: Since then, the world ___ through extraordinary changes.
items.why: Since then, up to now → present perfect.

items.text: There ___ no Internet until the 1990s.
In my parents' time, students ___ to the library to do research.
items.why: In my parents' time = finished → simple past.

items.text: Since the 1980s, computers and the Internet ___ communication dramatically.
items.why: Since the 1980s, up to now → present perfect.

items.text: Cell phones ___ available since the 1990s.
items.why: since … and still true → have been.

items.text: Texting ___ so popular that it has replaced phone calls for many people.
items.why: No time, result now → has become.

items.text: The first part of the story is about the 1950s. Why is it in the simple past?

talk.title: Then and now
talk.task: Write about how life has changed since your parents were young. Use simple past for then, present perfect for the changes.
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English writing partner. I am practicing simple past vs. present perfect. Ask me to choose one topic (communication, fashion, entertainment, transportation, or the environment) and write 3-4 sentences about how it was when my parents were young (simple past) and how it has changed since then (present perfect). Check that tense choice and help me keep sentences simple.

items.text: Since I came to this country, I [am learning] a lot about the way of life here.
options: Since I came to this country, I have learned a lot about the way of life here.
Since I came to this country, I learn a lot about the way of life here.
Since I came to this country, I had learned a lot about the way of life here.
items.why: Since … up to now → present perfect.

items.text: I [arrive] here only a short time ago.
options: I have arrived here only a short time ago.
I arrived here only a short time ago.
I am arriving here only a short time ago.

items.text: I [am] here since last Friday.
options: I was here since last Friday.
I am being here since last Friday.
I have been here since last Friday.
items.why: since last Friday, still true → have been.

items.text: How long [you are living] here?
options: How long are you living here?
How long have you been living here?
How long you have lived here?
items.why: How long, up to now → have you been living.

items.text: I [been] here for almost two years.
options: I have been here for almost two years.
I am here for almost two years.
I being here for almost two years.
items.why: been needs have: I have been.

items.text: Why [you no have been] in class for the last couple of days?
options: Why you haven't been in class for the last couple of days?
Why didn't you been in class for the last couple of days?

items.text: I [am coaching] a soccer team for the last two months.
options: I have been coaching a soccer team for the last two months.
I was coaching a soccer team for the last two months.
I coach a soccer team for the last two months.
items.why: for the last two months → have been coaching.

items.text: When I was a child, I [had lived] with my aunt instead of my parents.
options: When I was a child, I have lived with my aunt instead of my parents.
When I was a child, I lived with my aunt instead of my parents.
When I was a child, I had been living with my aunt instead of my parents.
items.why: One finished past time → simple past: lived.

items.text: My uncle [has die] before I [am] born, so I never knew him.
options: My uncle died before I am born, so I never knew him.
My uncle has died before I was born, so I never knew him.
My uncle had died before I was born, so I never knew him.
items.why: Earlier past: had died. Then: was born.

items.text: [I'm living] in my cousin's apartment since I [have arrived] here.
options: I've been living in my cousin's apartment since I arrived here.
I'm living in my cousin's apartment since I arrived here.
I've been living in my cousin's apartment since I have arrived here.
items.why: have been living … since + simple past.

items.text: [It very] small, and we are sharing the bedroom.
options: It very small, and we share the bedroom.
It is very small, and we are sharing the bedroom.
It has very small, and we are sharing the bedroom.
items.why: A sentence needs a verb: It is.

items.text: I [am needing] my own place, but I [don't find] one so far.
options: I need my own place, but I haven't found one so far.
I am needing my own place, but I haven't found one so far.
I need my own place, but I didn't find one so far.
items.why: need = state verb. so far → haven't found.

items.text: My grandfather [had lived] in a small village in Italy when he was a child.
options: My grandfather has lived in a small village in Italy when he was a child.
My grandfather had been living in a small village in Italy when he was a child.
My grandfather lived in a small village in Italy when he was a child.
items.why: One finished past time → simple past: lived.

items.text: At 19, he [had moved] to Rome, where he [had met] and [had married] my grandmother in 1957.
options: At 19, he moved to Rome, where he met and married my grandmother in 1957.
At 19, he has moved to Rome, where he has met and has married my grandmother in 1957.
At 19, he had moved to Rome, where he met and married my grandmother in 1957.
items.why: Events in time order → simple past.

items.text: My father [had been] born in Rome in 1960. I [am] born in Rome in 1989.
options: My father has been born in Rome in 1960. I was born in Rome in 1989.
My father was born in Rome in 1960. I was born in Rome in 1989.
My father was born in Rome in 1960. I am born in Rome in 1989.
items.why: in 1960 / in 1989 → simple past: was born.
